Example: "This reminds me of [thing] because [reason]"
Connections help you remember and understand the text
Before you read, look at the title and any pictures — what do you think it will be about?
As you read, pause and ask "What do I think will happen next?"
Write your prediction down
Keep reading to see if you were right
It doesn't matter if your prediction is wrong — the thinking is what helps
Good readers ask questions as they go
When something is confusing, write "I wonder..." in the margin
Example: "I wonder why the character did that"
Keep reading to see if the text answers your question
If not, look it up or ask your teacher
Start with a clear subject line: "Question about [topic]"
Open with "Dear [name]," or "Hi [name],"
State your purpose in the first sentence
Keep it brief — 3–5 sentences is usually enough
End with "Kind regards," or "Thanks," followed by your name
Read it once before sending to check for errors

title: Responding to an Important Text or Email

steps.text: Read the message fully before replying
Answer the actual question they asked — don't avoid it
Keep it clear and direct
If you need more time, reply: "Thanks — I'll come back to you on this by [date]"
Proofread before sending

title: When You Receive an Unwanted or Upsetting Message

steps.text: Step away from the screen before reacting
Don't reply while you're still upset — it often escalates things
Screenshot or save the message if it could be needed as evidence
Block, mute, or report if it's harassment
Talk to a trusted person before deciding what to do next
Before opening, check who it is — look through a peephole or window
Open the door and say "Hi, can I help you?" if it's an unfamiliar person
For someone you know: "Hey, come in!" and step aside
If it's an unexpected salesperson: "No thank you" and close the door — that's fine

title: Greeting Someone After a Long Time Apart

steps.text: It may feel awkward — that's completely normal
Say "It's so good to see you!" or "Wow, it's been a while!"
A hug or handshake is optional — follow their lead
Ask something simple: "How have you been?"
Listen and let the conversation warm up naturally

title: Greeting a New Teacher or Instructor

steps.text: Approach before class or during an appropriate moment
Say "Hi, I'm [your name] — this is my first time in your class"
Mention one relevant thing if helpful: "I learn better with written instructions"
Thank them for their time
Keep it brief — you can ask more questions as the course progresses
Wait for a natural moment — when you first see them or during a lull
Ask "How was your day?" and mean it
Listen to their answer — don't scroll your phone
React briefly: "That sounds tough" or "That's great!"
They will likely ask you back — share one highlight or lowlight
On Friday or Monday, this is a very common thing to ask
Say "Any plans this weekend?" or "How was your weekend?"
Listen to their answer and show interest
Share something brief about your own weekend if asked
Keep it light — this kind of small talk keeps relationships warm

title: Getting Out of an Awkward Silence

steps.text: Silences happen — they're less awkward than they feel
Try a light topic: "Have you been watching anything good lately?"
Or mention something in your environment: "I've been meaning to try this place"
If nothing works, it's fine to say "I should get going — good talking to you"

title: When You Don't Finish Schoolwork on Time

steps.text: Tell the teacher before the deadline — not after
Say "I'm sorry, I haven't finished my work — could I have more time?"
Give a brief, honest reason if you have one
Accept whatever they decide calmly
Complete it as soon as you can and don't leave it again
Wait until they've finished speaking
Say "I see it a bit differently — can I share my view?"
Use "I think..." rather than "You're wrong"
Explain your reasoning briefly
It's okay if you don't agree in the end — both views can exist

title: Dealing with an Unexpected Change at Work

steps.text: Take a breath when you hear about the change
Don't react out loud straight away — write down your initial reaction if needed
Ask for the information you need: "What does this mean for my role day-to-day?"
Focus on what you can control
Talk to a trusted person about how it's affecting you

title: Handling a Fire Drill or Unexpected Alarm

steps.text: Alarms are loud and sudden — try to stay calm
Stop what you're doing and follow other people out
Use the nearest fire exit — do not use the lift
Go to the assembly point and stay with your group
Wait for the all-clear before returning inside

title: Explaining Your Communication Style to Someone New

steps.text: Choose the right moment — not when things are rushed or tense
Say "I want to let you know how I communicate best"
Share what helps: "I prefer direct language" or "I need a moment to process before I respond"
You can add: "I'm not being rude — this is just how I work best"
Thank them for listening: "I really appreciate you knowing this"

title: Asking Someone to Speak More Slowly or Clearly

steps.text: You have every right to ask for communication that works for you
Say "Could you slow down a little? I want to make sure I understand"
Or: "Could you say that again more slowly?"
If they speak too quietly: "Sorry — could you speak up a bit?"
Most people won't mind — it shows you're listening carefully

title: Coping When Your Plans Change Unexpectedly

steps.text: Unexpected changes can feel very difficult — that reaction is valid
Take a slow breath before reacting
Say "I need a moment to adjust to this"
Write down the new plan to make it concrete
Identify one thing that's still the same as before
With time, the new plan will feel more familiar
Everyone makes social mistakes — autistic or not
Don't replay it obsessively — notice the thought and let it pass
If it affected someone, a brief apology is often enough: "I'm sorry if that came out wrong"
Remember: most people think about themselves, not your mistake, five minutes later
Ask yourself: "What would I tell a friend in this situation?" — then say it to yourself

title: Trying on Clothes in a Store

steps.text: Bring the items you want to the fitting room area
Ask the attendant "Can I use a changing room, please?"
They may count your items and give you a tag
Try the items and keep everything else on a hanger
Return unwanted items to the attendant — don't leave them in the room

title: When a Sales Associate Approaches You

steps.text: They'll often say "Can I help you find anything?"
If you want help: "Yes — I'm looking for [item]"
If you're just browsing, say "No thanks, just looking" — that's fine
You don't need to explain yourself further

title: When Something Breaks Quickly After Buying It

steps.text: Keep your receipt — it's your proof of purchase
Return to the store and explain calmly: "I bought this [X] days ago and it's already stopped working"
Ask "Am I entitled to a replacement or refund?"
In most countries, consumer law protects you for faulty goods
If they refuse, ask to speak to a manager or contact consumer advice

title: Preparing a Health Appointment as an Autistic Person

steps.text: Write down your symptoms, concerns, and any questions in advance
You can bring a support person or ask them to join by phone
Tell the doctor at the start: "I'm autistic — I may need information repeated or written down"
Don't minimise symptoms — describe them as clearly as you can
Ask for a written summary of the appointment or next steps
Find the appropriate aisle, or ask staff to point you to it
Read labels carefully for dosage and age suitability
If unsure, ask the pharmacist: "Is this appropriate for [condition]?"
Tell them of any other medications you take: "I also take [medication] — is this safe?"
Take only the recommended amount

title: Telling a Professional About Masking or Camouflaging

steps.text: Masking — hiding autistic traits — is exhausting and valid to talk about
Say "I want to tell you about something called masking"
Explain: "I often hide how I'm actually feeling or what I need to fit in"
Tell them the impact: "It leaves me exhausted and I'm not always honest about my difficulties"
Ask: "Can we work on strategies so I don't have to do this as much?"

title: Saying No to an Offer of Food or Drink

steps.text: It's always okay to decline food or drink
Say "No thank you — I'm fine for now"
If they ask why, you don't need to give a detailed reason: "I'm just not hungry, thanks"
Don't feel pressured to eat or drink to be polite — your body is yours

title: When You Feel Manipulated or Guilted

steps.text: Notice the signs: someone making you feel bad for having a boundary
Stay calm and don't be drawn into justifying yourself
Say "I hear that you're upset, but my answer is still no"
You don't owe anyone an explanation for a decision about your own life
Walk away if the pressure continues
Write down your early warning signs — what does overwhelm feel like for you?
List 3 things that help you regulate: headphones, walking, breathing, cold water
Identify 2 safe people you can contact when struggling
Write down your go-to exit strategies for different places
Keep this plan somewhere accessible — phone, wallet, or bag

title: Reporting a Problem to a Staff Member

steps.text: Find someone in a uniform or with an ID badge
Say "Excuse me — I need to report something"
Describe the problem clearly: what happened, where, and when
Give as much detail as you can without adding opinion
Ask "What happens next?" so you know what to expect

title: Asking Your Teacher for Help After Class

steps.text: Wait until other students have left or there's a quiet moment
Say "Excuse me — do you have a moment? I had a question about [topic]"
Explain specifically what you don't understand
Listen carefully and take notes
Thank them: "That makes a lot more sense now — thank you"

title: When You Don't Understand Sarcasm or a Joke

steps.text: It's okay to ask — not everyone understands every type of humour
Say "Sorry — were you joking there, or do you mean that literally?"
Or: "I'm not sure if I got that — can you explain?"
Most people find this endearing rather than awkward
Once you know, you can decide how to respond

title: When You Feel Anxious in a New Environment

steps.text: New places can feel uncertain — take it slowly
Find one familiar or predictable thing to anchor to
Breathe slowly and move at your own pace
Give yourself permission to leave if you need to
Each time you return, it will feel more familiar

title: When Someone Asks "Are You Okay?" and You're Not

steps.text: You don't have to say "fine" if you're not
You can say "Not really, but I'm managing"
Or: "I'm having a bit of a hard time at the moment"
If you want to talk: "Would you have a moment to listen?"
If not: "I'd rather not get into it right now, but thanks for asking"

title: Asking to Sit with Someone at Lunch

steps.text: Look for someone who has space next to them
Approach and ask "Is anyone sitting here?"
If they say yes: "Do you mind if I sit here?"
Sit down and you don't have to talk — eating quietly next to someone is fine
If they start talking, respond briefly and warmly
If you notice they seem upset or the conversation went quiet — check in
Say "I'm sorry — I think what I said might have come across badly"
Clarify what you meant: "I didn't mean it that way — I meant [X]"
Listen to how they took it without getting defensive
Thank them for telling you: "I'm glad I know — I'll be more careful"
Give yourself time to adjust — it's completely normal to find change hard
Explore the area in small steps: the nearest shop, park, transport stop
Find the routines that anchor you: a regular coffee spot, a walking route
Introduce yourself to immediate neighbours when you're ready: "Hi, I've just moved in next door"
Look for a local group or club connected to your interests

title: Attending a Religious or Cultural Service

steps.text: Research what to expect and any dress code in advance
Arrive a few minutes early and find a seat near an exit if that helps
Follow the lead of others: stand, sit, and move when they do
If you're unsure of something, it's fine to stay seated quietly
At the end, a simple "Thank you" to a greeter is always appreciated

title: Reminding Someone About an Appointment or Event

steps.text: Send a brief message a day or two beforehand
Say "Just a reminder about [event] on [day] at [time]"
Include the location if helpful
Ask "Does that still work for you?"
A short, friendly reminder is helpful — not annoying

title: Sending an Apology by Text or Email

steps.text: Sometimes a written apology is easier to express clearly
Start with "I wanted to apologise for [what happened]"
Keep it brief and genuine — don't over-explain
Don't add "but" — it undoes the apology
End with "I hope we're okay" or "Let me know if you want to talk"

title: Asking About Side Effects of a Medication

steps.text: You have the right to know about what you're taking
Ask the pharmacist or doctor: "What side effects should I know about?"
Ask: "When should I be concerned and contact you?"
Write down the answers or ask for a leaflet
If you notice something unusual, report it — don't just stop the medication
You always have the right to seek a second medical opinion
Ask your current doctor: "Is it possible to get a second opinion on this?"
Or contact another clinic and say "I'd like a second opinion on [condition]"
Request copies of your records and test results
This isn't disrespectful — it's a normal part of healthcare
Some topics are private and you don't have to discuss them
Say "That's a bit personal — I'd rather not get into it"
Or: "I prefer to keep that private"
You don't need to apologise for having privacy
Change the subject: "Anyway, how about you — what's new with you?"

title: Telling Someone About Your Sensory Needs

steps.text: Your sensory needs are valid and worth communicating
Pick a calm moment — not in the middle of a social situation
Say "I want to let you know that I'm sensitive to [loud sounds / touch / smells, etc.]"
Tell them what helps: "If [thing] is happening, I may need to step away"
Thank them for understanding: "I appreciate you knowing this about me"

title: Following Up After a Job Application

steps.text: Wait at least a week after the deadline before following up
Send a brief email: "Hi, I'm writing to follow up on my application for [role]"
Say "I remain very interested and wanted to check on the timeline"
Keep it short — 3–4 sentences maximum
Sign off professionally: "Thank you for your time — [your name]"

title: Asking Your Manager for Regular Check-Ins

steps.text: Regular feedback helps you know you're on track
Say "I work best when I have regular feedback — could we schedule a brief weekly check-in?"
Suggest a format: "Even 10 minutes would help me stay aligned with priorities"
Most good managers will welcome this — it shows initiative
Many people process written information better — you're not alone
Say "Could I have those instructions in writing too? It helps me make sure I get everything right"
Or: "Could you email that to me so I can refer back to it?"
This is a reasonable request and most teachers and managers will agree

title: Telling a New Friend You Are Autistic

steps.text: Disclosure is your choice — there's no right or wrong time
Choose someone you feel comfortable with and a calm setting
Say "There's something I'd like to share — I'm autistic"
You can explain what that means for you: "For me it means [X]"
Answer any questions honestly and calmly
A good friend will appreciate your trust and want to understand
Stimming is a natural and valid way to self-regulate
If someone comments, say calmly: "This is something I do to help manage my senses"
Or: "It helps me focus and stay calm"
You don't owe anyone a detailed explanation
If they're respectful and curious, you can share more if you choose

title: When You're Overwhelmed by Social Expectations

steps.text: Social rules can feel confusing and exhausting — that's valid
Remind yourself: you don't have to do everything perfectly
Focus on one interaction at a time, not all the rules at once
Give yourself recovery time after intense social events — it's not weakness
Talk to a therapist or trusted person about what's hardest
Personal space is an arm's length around each person
When talking to someone, stay at a comfortable distance — about arm's length
If they step back, don't step closer
If someone is too close to you, step back or say "Could you give me a little more space?"
Online: personal space means not messaging someone repeatedly before they reply
If something belongs to everyone, take turns using it
Ask before picking something up that belongs to another person
If someone asks to use yours, you can share or say "I'm using it right now — you can have a go when I'm done"
Sharing doesn't mean giving something away forever
Return borrowed things in good condition
Use the cubicle for privacy — lock the door
Flush when done
Wash your hands with soap for at least 20 seconds
Dry your hands and dispose of paper towels in the bin
Leave the space as you found it for the next person

title: Knowing Where to Find Bathrooms in Different Places

steps.text: In a shop or restaurant: look for signs or ask staff
In a library, museum or cinema: look for signs near the entrance
On a bus or train: ask the driver/guard
In an airport: they are very well signed throughout
It's okay to ask — everyone needs the bathroom
One clear apology is usually enough — repeating it can make things more awkward
Say "I'm sorry for [specific thing]" once and clearly
Don't say "I'm so, so sorry, I'm terrible" — it shifts the focus to you
After apologising, move forward — don't keep bringing it up
Showing change through your actions is more powerful than repeated words
Book the ride in the app — confirm the destination before requesting
Wait at the pickup spot shown in the app
Check the driver's name, car, and plate number match the app
Greet briefly: "Hi" is enough — you don't have to chat
Rate the driver after the trip if prompted

title: Starting and Ending a Work Shift

steps.text: Arrive a few minutes early and sign in if required
Say a brief "Good morning" to your team
Check for any messages or updates before starting your tasks
At the end of your shift, complete any handover and log out
Say "See you tomorrow" or "Goodbye" to those nearby

title: How to Say Sorry to a Friend

steps.text: Think about what you did that hurt them
Choose a calm moment — not when you're still upset
Say "I'm sorry for [what you did]"
Don't add "but" — a real apology doesn't have conditions
Ask "Are you okay?" and listen to what they say
Give them space if they need time

title: Apologizing When You Hurt Someone by Accident

steps.text: Even accidents can hurt feelings — apologizing still matters
Say "I'm sorry — I didn't mean to do that"
Ask "Are you okay?"
Listen to their answer and don't rush to defend yourself
Offer to help if you can fix the situation

title: What to Do When You Make a Mistake

steps.text: Everyone makes mistakes — they don't make you a bad person
Take a breath and notice what went wrong
Say "I made a mistake. I need to fix it."
Do what you can to put it right
Learn from it and let it go — you don't have to dwell on it

title: When You Break or Lose Someone's Belonging

steps.text: Tell them as soon as possible — the longer you wait, the harder it gets
Say "I'm really sorry — I broke/lost your [item]"
Be honest about what happened
Offer to replace or repair it if you can
Accept their feelings — they may be upset and that's fair

title: Accepting an Apology from Someone Else

steps.text: Take a moment before you respond
If you're ready to forgive, say "Thank you for apologizing" or "It's okay"
If you're not ready, it's okay to say "I need a bit more time"
You don't have to pretend the hurt didn't happen
Forgiveness is a process — it doesn't have to be immediate
Find a private or quiet moment to apologize
Say "I want to apologize for [what happened]"
Be specific and brief — don't over-explain
Say "It won't happen again"
If appropriate: "What can I do to make it right?"
Losing feels hard — that's normal, it's okay to feel it
Take a slow breath before you react
Say "Good game" or "Well played" to the winner
Try not to talk about what went wrong right away
If you want a rematch, ask calmly: "Want to play again?"
Winning feels good — it's fine to be happy inside
Say "Good game" instead of announcing you won loudly
Don't replay winning moments or explain how the other person lost
Ask if they want to play again
Being a fair winner makes people want to play with you again
Look around to see who else is there and what they're doing
Wait your turn for equipment — others are there too
If you want to join a game, ask: "Can I play too?"
Be gentle and don't push — everyone has the right to feel safe
If someone is being unkind, walk away and tell an adult

title: Asking to Join a Game Already in Progress

steps.text: Watch the game for a moment to understand the rules
Wait for a natural pause in the action
Say "That looks fun — can I join in?"
Accept the answer — if it's no, that's okay. Try again another time.
If yes, ask about any rules you're not sure about
Wait for the other person to finish their turn
Keep track of whose turn it is — you can say it out loud: "My turn, then yours"
If you forget, ask calmly: "Whose turn is it?"
Cheer for the other player sometimes — it feels good for both of you
Notice the feeling in your body — is it getting too intense?
Take a deep breath and pause for a moment
You can say "I need a second" — short breaks are okay
Ask yourself: "Is it worth staying upset?" — usually the answer is no
If you need to stop playing, say "I want to take a break from this game"

title: When Someone Doesn't Follow the Rules

steps.text: Stay calm — getting angry usually makes things worse
Say "I think the rule is [X] — can we check?"
Suggest looking up the rules together if you're unsure
If they keep bending rules, you can say "It's not as fun when rules aren't followed"
You can choose not to play — it's okay to stop a game
Sit down at the table when it's time to eat
Wait until everyone is served before starting if that's the custom
Chew with your mouth closed and don't talk while swallowing
Say "Please" when asking for something and "Thank you" when you receive it
If you don't like something, you can say "No thank you"
Use an indoor voice — restaurants are shared spaces
Keep your phone down unless needed
Use utensils rather than fingers when expected
Say "Excuse me" to get a waiter's attention — don't click or shout
Wait for everyone to be served before eating, if you can
Say "Thank you" when plates are cleared or drinks are refilled
Cover your mouth and nose with your elbow or a tissue
Turn away from people if you can
Say "Excuse me" after you sneeze or cough
Dispose of the tissue and wash or sanitise your hands
If you're unwell, wear a mask or give people extra space

title: When Your Body Makes an Embarrassing Noise

steps.text: Bodies sometimes make noises — it happens to everyone
Say "Excuse me" quietly
Don't bring a lot of attention to it
If someone makes a big deal about it, you can say "It happens to everyone"

title: Waiting Your Turn in a Queue

steps.text: Find the back of the line and join there
Keep a body-width of space between you and the person ahead
Wait patiently — everyone is waiting too
If someone cuts in front, you can say "Excuse me, I was next"
Be ready when it's your turn so the queue moves faster for everyone

title: Holding a Door Open for Someone

steps.text: If someone is close behind you at a door, hold it open briefly
You don't have to hold it for very long — just enough so it doesn't close on them
They will usually say "Thank you"
Nod or say "No problem" or just smile

title: Good Manners as a Guest at Someone's Home

steps.text: Take off your shoes at the door unless told otherwise
Say "Thank you for having me" when you arrive
Ask before touching or using things that aren't yours
Help tidy up after meals if you can
Before you leave, say "Thank you — I had a really nice time"

title: Receiving a Gift You Don't Like

steps.text: The person put effort into thinking of you — that matters
Smile and say "Thank you, that's really kind of you"
Find something true and positive to say: "I love the colour" or "That was thoughtful"
You don't have to lie about loving it, but you don't need to say you dislike it either
Keep your reaction brief — then move the conversation on
It's wonderful to show genuine excitement!
Say "Thank you so much — I love this!"
Tell them specifically why you like it if you can
Giving a hug or high-five is optional — whatever feels natural for you
Hand the gift over and say "This is for you"
You can add "I thought you might like it" or "Happy birthday!"
Wait while they open it — watch their reaction without staring
If they thank you, say "I'm glad you like it" or "You're welcome"
Go with a trusted adult or group — safety first
Knock or ring the doorbell and wait
When the door opens, say "Trick or treat!"
Hold out your bag or bucket when they offer sweets
Say "Thank you!" and move on — don't linger or ask for more
If no one answers, that's fine — just go to the next house
Arrive close to the start time — not too early or very late
Say "Happy birthday!" to the birthday person when you see them
Give the gift and let them open it in their own time
Try to join in at least one activity — even briefly is okay
If it feels overwhelming, it's okay to take a quiet break
Before you leave, thank the host: "Thanks for inviting me"

title: When a Holiday Celebration Feels Overwhelming

steps.text: Big gatherings can be loud and unpredictable — plan for it
Find a quiet spot to retreat to if you need a break
It's okay to say "I'm going to get some air" and step outside briefly
Have a signal with a trusted person if you need to leave early
You don't have to stay the whole time

title: Asking Someone to Be Your Friend

steps.text: Find someone you've talked to a few times or have things in common with
Ask "Do you want to hang out sometime?"
Suggest something specific: "We could play [game] or walk to [place]"
If they say yes — great! Make a plan
If they say no or seem unsure, that's okay — not everyone will connect with you, and that's normal

title: Inviting Someone to Do Something Together

steps.text: Think of an activity you'd both enjoy
Say "I was thinking of [activity] — would you want to come?"
Give them a specific time: "Maybe Saturday afternoon?"
Accept their answer without pressure
If they say yes, confirm the details before the day
Notice the difference: friendly teasing vs. mean teasing
If it bothers you, say calmly: "I don't like being teased about that"
If they continue, walk away — you don't have to stay
Tell a trusted adult or friend if it keeps happening
Teasing that upsets you regularly is bullying and you deserve help

title: When You See Someone Being Bullied

steps.text: Don't join in or ignore it — both make things worse
If it's safe: stand next to the person being bullied
Say to the bully: "That's not cool — stop it"
Tell a trusted adult what happened
Later, check in with the person: "Are you okay? I saw what happened"

title: Helping a Friend Who Is Upset

steps.text: Notice when a friend seems sad, quiet, or different than usual
Ask gently: "Are you okay? You seem a bit quiet today"
Listen without trying to fix it or give advice straight away
You can say "That sounds really hard. I'm here for you"
Ask "Is there anything I can do to help?"
If you're worried about their safety, tell a trusted adult
If you always make the effort and they don't, notice that pattern
Find a calm moment and say "I feel like I'm always the one reaching out"
Ask "Is everything okay between us?"
Listen to their response — they might not have realised
Good friendships work both ways — it's okay to say that
You have the right to say no to anything that makes you uncomfortable
Say "No thanks, that's not for me"
If they push back, say "I said no — please respect that"
Real friends won't pressure you
Walk away and, if needed, tell a trusted person what happened

title: When Someone Is Mean to You Online

steps.text: Don't respond right away — step away from the screen first
Screenshot or save the message as evidence
Block or mute the person if you need to
Tell a trusted adult — online unkindness is still real unkindness
You don't have to figure this out alone

title: When You Feel Frustrated or Angry

steps.text: Notice the feeling in your body — tight chest, hot face, clenched hands
Take a slow breath in for 4 counts, out for 6
Walk away from the situation if you can
Do something physical — walk, jump, squeeze something
When calmer, think about what happened and how to handle it

title: When You Feel Nervous or Anxious Before an Event

steps.text: Feeling nervous is normal — your brain is trying to prepare you
Breathe slowly — in through the nose, out through the mouth
Think of one thing you're looking forward to, even something small
Remember: you have managed difficult situations before
If it helps, tell someone you trust: "I'm feeling nervous about [event]"
It's okay not to like something — you don't have to pretend
In a public or group setting, stay quiet if possible — not every opinion needs to be shared aloud
If asked, you can say "It's not really my thing, but I can see why others enjoy it"
If it's something that directly affects you, it's okay to speak up politely

title: Sharing Excitement About Something You Love

steps.text: It's wonderful to share things you're passionate about
Share the most interesting part first — not the full background
Watch their reactions: are they engaged or looking away?
Ask them a question about it to invite them in
If they're not interested, that's okay — not everyone shares our interests
It's painful to feel left out — that feeling is valid
Take a moment before reacting — don't assume it was intentional
You can ask calmly: "I noticed I wasn't included — was there a reason?"
If it keeps happening, talk to a trusted person about how you feel
Remember: one group isn't the only source of connection
Disappointment means you cared — that's not a weakness
Take a breath and name the feeling: "I'm disappointed because [X]"
Don't make big decisions while feeling it strongly
Talk to someone you trust about how you feel
With time, a different path or opportunity will appear

title: When Everything Feels Like Too Much

steps.text: Stop what you're doing — you need a pause
Find a quiet, safe place if you can
Breathe slowly and deeply until your heart rate settles
Do something grounding: name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch
When ready, decide on ONE small next step — just one
Talk to someone you trust about how you're feeling
Take a breath before reacting
Say "I don't think I explained myself clearly — can I try again?"
Use different words or an example to explain what you meant
Check: "Does that make more sense?"
If they still don't understand, it's okay to say "That's okay — maybe we can talk about it more another time"
Use a quiet, indoor voice — this is a quiet shared space
Books are organised by genre or author — ask staff if you're unsure
Handle books carefully and return them to where you got them
If you want to borrow a book, take it to the self-serve machine or desk
Keep your library card with you
Find a librarian — they're usually at the desk or shelving books
Say "Excuse me, could you help me find something?"
Describe what you're looking for: title, author, or topic
Thank them and follow their directions
Check the due date — returning on time avoids fines
Use the book return slot or bring it to the desk
If you have a fine, pay it calmly at the desk: "I have an overdue fine — can I pay it?"
Ask for a receipt if you want proof the book was returned

title: Using a Library Computer or Study Area

steps.text: Check if you need to book the computer or if it's walk-in
Log in with your library card number if prompted
Keep your volume down — headphones are best for audio
Log out and clear the session when you're done
Leave the area tidy for the next person
Have the date, time, and number of people ready before you call
Say "Hi, I'd like to make a reservation for [number] people on [date] at [time]"
If you have dietary needs, mention them now: "One person is vegetarian"
Give your name and phone number
Confirm the booking details before hanging up

title: Arriving and Being Seated at a Restaurant

steps.text: Wait at the entrance for a staff member to greet you
Say "Hi, I have a reservation under [your name]" or "Table for [number], please"
Follow them to your table
If the table isn't comfortable (too loud, cold, etc.) it's okay to ask: "Is it possible to sit somewhere quieter?"

title: Asking About Allergens or Dietary Needs

steps.text: Mention your allergy or dietary need clearly and calmly
Say "I have a [allergy/dietary need] — can you tell me which dishes are suitable?"
Ask "Is this dish prepared near [allergen]?" if needed
Confirm with the server before ordering: "You've noted the [allergy], right?"
Don't feel embarrassed — your safety is the priority

title: Paying the Bill at a Restaurant

steps.text: When ready to pay, catch the server's eye or say "Excuse me — could we get the bill?"
Check the bill matches what you ordered
If something is wrong, say "I think there's an error — I didn't order [X]"
Pay by card or cash — tap or insert when prompted
A tip of 10–15% is customary in many places, but always optional

title: When Your Food Takes Too Long

steps.text: Give it a reasonable time — kitchens can be busy
After 20–30 minutes, catch the server's attention with a wave or "Excuse me"
Say "We've been waiting a while — could you check on our order?"
Stay calm and polite — making a scene rarely helps
They will usually apologise and give you an update
Decide before ordering whether you're splitting equally or paying for your own
When the bill arrives, divide the total by the number of people if splitting equally
Or add up what you personally ordered
Pay your share and include a portion of any tip
If anyone is short, cover them quietly and sort it out later

title: Eating Out with Specific Sensory Needs

steps.text: Choose restaurants in advance — look up the menu and noise level online
Book a table in a quieter area if possible, e.g. "away from the kitchen"
It's okay to bring ear defenders or sensory tools
You can ask the server: "Could you bring [dish] without [ingredient]?"
Have a plan: know where the exit is and where you can take a quiet break

title: Planning a Journey on Public Transport

steps.text: Use Google Maps, Citymapper or a local app to plan your route
Check the departure time and leave early enough
Know your destination stop and the number of stops if helpful
Charge your phone and download the route offline if you might lose signal
Have a backup plan: who to call if something goes wrong

title: Buying a Bus or Train Ticket

steps.text: Find the ticket machine or buy online before you go
Select your destination, journey type, and number of tickets
Pay by card or cash
Keep the ticket until you exit — some systems check on the way out too
If confused at the machine, ask a staff member nearby

title: Using a Train Station for the First Time

steps.text: Find the departures board — it shows platform numbers and times
Head to your platform with plenty of time
Check the sign on the train confirms your destination
Board when the doors open and find a seat
If unsure, ask a guard or fellow passenger: "Is this the train to [city]?"

title: When Your Bus or Train Is Delayed

steps.text: Check the app or departures board for an update
Wait in a safe, comfortable spot
If you're meeting someone, text them: "My train is delayed — I'll be [time] late"
If the delay is very long, ask staff about alternatives
Stay calm — delays are frustrating but usually resolve
Arrive at the airport at least 2 hours before departure
Check in online in advance to save time
Follow the security signs: remove shoes, put liquids in a bag
Find your departure gate from the screens
Board when your zone or row is called
Follow crew instructions and let them know if you need any support
Parks are shared spaces — be mindful of others
Pick up after yourself and your dog if you have one
Give people space — sit at a distance from others unless the park is full
If you want to use a bench someone is near, it's fine to sit — a nod is enough
Enjoy the outdoors at your own pace

title: Joining a Fitness Class for the First Time

steps.text: Arrive 5 minutes early to set up and let the instructor know you're new
Say "Hi, it's my first time — any advice?"
Pick a spot where you can see the instructor clearly
It's okay to go at your own pace and modify moves
You don't need to chat to others — focus on the class

title: Using a Gym for the First Time

steps.text: Ask for an induction when you join — most gyms offer one
Wipe down equipment after use with the provided spray and cloth
Put weights back where you found them
Don't use equipment you haven't been shown — ask staff first
Headphones make it easier to exercise without small talk
Book your ticket in advance to choose your seat
Arrive a few minutes early — ads play before the film
Turn your phone on silent before the film starts
Eat quietly and avoid loud crunching during quiet scenes if possible
Stay seated until the credits end if you want to avoid the crowd
Many museums are free — check online before you go
Use an indoor voice and don't touch exhibits unless signs say you can
Take a map at the entrance to plan your route
Take breaks — it's fine to sit down or step outside
If it gets overwhelming, you can always leave and come back another day

title: Attending a Community Event or Festival

steps.text: Look up the event in advance — what's there, how loud, how crowded
Bring ear defenders, sunglasses, or anything that helps your senses
Have a plan: know where the exits and quiet areas are
Go with someone you trust if possible
It's always okay to leave early
Use an ATM in a well-lit, public place
Insert your card chip-first and enter your PIN (shield the keypad)
Select "Withdraw cash" and choose the amount
Take your card first, then the cash and receipt
Put everything away before walking away
Bring ID and any relevant documents
Take a number ticket if there's a queue system
When called, go to the counter and say "I'd like to [task]"
Answer their security questions clearly
Ask for clarification if you don't understand something
Take any paperwork or receipts they give you

title: Sending a Package at the Post Office

steps.text: Pack and seal your item before you arrive
Write the address clearly on the outside or use a printed label
At the counter, say "I'd like to send this please"
Choose standard, tracked, or express — staff can advise
Pay and keep your tracking receipt

title: Collecting a Parcel from the Post Office

steps.text: Bring your collection card or notification and photo ID
Go to the counter and say "I'm here to collect a parcel"
Show your ID and sign if asked
Check the parcel is undamaged before you leave
Scan the menu before stepping up to the counter
When it's your turn, say your order clearly: "Can I have a [drink] and [food] please?"
Mention customisations: "Oat milk, please" or "No ice"
Give your name if asked and move aside to wait
Collect your order when your name is called and say "Thank you"

title: Asking About Allergens in a Café

steps.text: You have the right to ask about ingredients — don't hesitate
Say "I have a [allergy] — could you check if [item] contains it?"
If they're unsure, ask "Is there someone who would know?"
If they can't confirm it's safe, choose something else

title: Staying to Work or Study in a Café

steps.text: Buy something when you sit down — it's polite if you're staying long
Use headphones and keep your voice down if on calls
Don't spread across multiple seats during busy periods
Buy another item if you plan to stay more than an hour
Tidy your space when you leave

title: When Your Café Order Is Wrong

steps.text: Go back to the counter calmly
Say "Excuse me, I think my order might be wrong"
Describe what you got vs what you ordered
They will usually fix it without fuss
Say "Thank you" when they bring the correct order
Wait for a free machine and go when it's clear
Scan each item — place it in the bag after scanning
If an item doesn't scan, try again or call for assistance
Select "Finish & Pay" when done and pay by card or cash
Take your receipt and bags

title: When the Store Is Very Crowded

steps.text: Shop at quieter times if possible: early morning or late evening
Use a list so you can move through quickly
Breathe slowly if you start to feel overwhelmed
If it's too much, leave your basket and step outside for fresh air
You can always come back later — you don't have to push through

title: Asking for Help at the Deli or Bakery Counter

steps.text: Wait to be served — take a number if there's a system
Say what you'd like clearly: "Could I have 200g of [item] please?"
If you're unsure about quantities, it's fine to say "About this much" and show with your hands
Check the amount when they show you, before they wrap it
Say "Thank you" when they hand it over

title: When an Item Scans at the Wrong Price

steps.text: Stay calm — pricing errors do happen
Say to the cashier "I think this item was priced differently on the shelf"
They may need to call a colleague to check
Show the shelf photo or describe where you found it
In most places, the shelf price is the one they'll honour
Pay at reception and show your membership if you have one
Find the changing rooms — there are usually separate rooms or mixed family changing
Use a locker for your belongings and take the key with you
Shower briefly before entering the pool — it's usually required
Read any lane signs: "slow", "medium", "fast" — pick the right one
No running on the poolside — the floor is slippery
Swim on the left side of your lane — let faster swimmers pass
Wait at the end of the lane if someone is doing a tumble turn
Don't splash others deliberately
Follow the lifeguard's instructions immediately
Use a private cubicle if available and that feels more comfortable
Keep your belongings in your locker or bag — don't spread out
Allow space for others — don't block sinks or exits
Leave the space tidy and free of wet towels on the floor

title: Visiting a Friend's Home for the First Time

steps.text: Arrive at the agreed time — not too early
Say "Thanks for inviting me" when you arrive
Follow their lead — remove shoes if they do, sit where offered
Ask before exploring or using things: "Is it okay if I use the bathroom?"
When you leave, say "I really enjoyed this — thanks for having me"

title: Attending a Wedding or Formal Event

steps.text: Check the dress code and plan your outfit in advance
Arrive on time — formal events often run to a strict schedule
Turn your phone fully silent
Follow the schedule: sit where directed, stand when others do
At a reception, you don't need to talk to everyone — small interactions are enough
Before leaving, congratulate the main people: "Congratulations — it was beautiful"

title: First Day at a New Job

steps.text: Arrive on time and go to the reception or main entrance
Say "Hi, I'm [your name] — it's my first day"
Observe and listen more than you speak on the first day
Write down names, processes, and important information
Ask one or two questions — not too many at once
At the end, say "Thanks everyone — I'm looking forward to getting started"

title: Talking to Someone at a Party When You Don't Know Many People

steps.text: Find someone who looks friendly and is also standing alone
Approach and say "Hi, I'm [your name] — how do you know [host]?"
Listen to their answer and ask a follow-up question
Share a little about yourself too
If it goes quiet, it's okay to say "I'll go grab a drink — nice to meet you"

title: Splitting a Bill at a Restaurant

steps.text: When the bill comes, say "Shall we split it?" or "Can we have separate bills?"
If splitting, divide the total by the number of people or by what you ordered
Pay your share by card or cash
